So I've been a big backpacker the last decade or so. Primarily I started out packing medium weight in the mid 2000s with canned foods, granola bars, protein bars, fresh fruit, some trail mix. Last 3 years I've been using a jet boil with freeze dried entrees(mountain house, backpackers pantry, alpine aire). I probably got 30 or so packs left with best before 2020-2027 although some of the mountain house ones are probably 30+ years. But for the life of me I've never actually seen an MRE. When I was in the reserves sometimes we had our own IMP packs which is a Canadian military version. Not once have a seen a genuine MRE or any real MREs for sale up here. I have seen some meal kit supply cases for sale on amazon.ca but they are kind of expensive. So how the fuck do people get their hands on these? And do the commercial meal kit supply or xmre ones hold up?

The official ones are only given out by the military. I used to get them from my dad back in the day, and later from a friend in the Marines. I'm not sure if food rations wind up in surplus shops. I do know there are a couple of companies that use the same brands of items that the official MRE's do (XMRE I believe?) and even use the same black-and-tan packaging.

And from what I've seen, the commercial packs usually beat out the official military ones...as you might expect.

I got some mountain house stuff for camping and from what I was told they supply the LRP/MCW mains for the special forces but it isn't the same. I tried contacting the meal kit supply vendor on amazon and I haven't got a response to when their product will be available again. Might be better to just keep buying a mix of canned from superstore and freeze dried from MEC when I head out next month

The first 4-5 minutes about the actual Gameboy were cool. The last 5 minutes were basically a lesson in Assembly programming that has almost nothing to do with the actual Gameboy (outside of the fact the gameboy ran on it).
I think the idea was to only explain some of the challenges required in making a GB game while demonstrating just how limited the hardware is.

Kids interested in computers are often linked to programming because of games. Technical kids are often interested in retro hardware, especially due to its availability and the ability to control it. With the high production value of this video I imagine that is the target audience. This is an awesome introductory video to present assembly programming in a way certain 12 year olds will eat it up.
